title: Ripple Chevron Shawl
subtitle: Traditional ripple stitch triangle in aran weight, increasing from the top down
excerpt: A triangular shawl worked in the classic ripple stitch: paired increases form the peaks and paired decreases form the valleys of each chevron row. Aran weight on a 5mm hook produces a bold, structured fabric with clear directional movement.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Ripple chevron stitch is a well-established crochet technique with no single originating source.

glossaryTerms.definition: A row pattern that alternates increases and decreases at regular intervals to create a zigzag wave across the fabric.
Treble two together: begin two trebles into separate stitches but stop at the last yarn-over step, then pull through all three loops to join them at the top.

content.text: This shawl is a top-down triangle measuring approximately 155cm across the top edge and 70cm from the top to the lower point. It is worked in the traditional ripple stitch: each row has alternating peaks, where you place 3 trebles into one stitch, and valleys, where you work two trebles together twice in succession. The triangle grows because the outer two stitches of every row are worked as increases rather than as decreases, adding one peak at each side on every other row. Aran weight yarn on a 5mm hook produces a firm, structured fabric with bold chevron movement. The pattern requires counting carefully: each peak and each valley must occur in the correct place for the chevron columns to align.

Yarn: approximately 550g of aran weight yarn. A smooth, lightly spun yarn shows the chevron ridges well. Hook: 5mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, a tape measure, and optional stitch markers, blocking mat, and rust-proof pins.

One ripple repeat (10 stitches) measures approximately 7cm wide and 2 rows measure approximately 5cm in height, using a 5mm hook over aran weight ripple stitch. Work a flat swatch of at least 30 stitches to check your tension before starting the full triangle.
Ripple: alternating 3-in-1 increases and tr2tog decreases

Each ripple repeat is 10 stitches: 3 tr at the peak, tr2tog twice for the valley (consuming 4 stitches but creating 2), then 3 tr at the next peak. The triangle starts with one small repeat and grows by adding a repeat at each edge on every increase row. The ch-3 turning chain counts as the first tr throughout.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr in 4th ch from hook (peak start), tr in next 3 ch, tr2tog twice (valley), tr in next 3 ch, 3 tr in last ch (peak end), turn. (13 sts)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr in first st (edge increase), tr in next 3 sts, tr2tog twice (valley), tr in next 3 sts, 3 tr in last st (edge peak), turn. (13 sts)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 3 tr in first st (outer peak added), tr in next 3 sts, [tr2tog twice, tr in next 3 sts, 3 tr in peak st, tr in next 3 sts] across, 3 tr in top of turning ch, turn. (add 2 extra sts at each edge: approximately 17 sts)

On every RS (odd) row, add a new peak at each outer edge by working 3 tr into the first st and 3 tr into the top of the final turning ch. On every WS (even) row, maintain the stitch count by working 2 tr at each outer edge. The valley positions stay fixed within each repeat. Continue adding repeats until the top edge measures approximately 155cm, ending on a WS row.

At the stated gauge, approximately 22 full ripple repeats across the top row gives a 155cm edge width. This requires approximately 44 total rows. Check width against the tape measure after every 10 rows and adjust if your tension differs.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Block firmly: soak in cool water, remove excess moisture in a towel, then pin the top edge to 155cm and the lower point to 70cm depth on a foam mat. The ripple chevrons need pinning at each peak and valley along the lower edge to set the wave. Allow to dry completely.
Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Reshape and dry flat. Do not tumble dry or wring. Re-block after washing if the chevron definition softens.

Ripple stitch in a flat rectangle is a natural next step: all the decreases and increases remain but there is no shaping to track. A multicolour ripple blanket uses exactly this approach and lets you practise stripe colour-changes. For a triangle with a single clean increase line rather than chevron movement, the asymmetric wedge shawl uses dc rows with one increase at one edge only.
